papers.title: Counterfactual effect of Colombian protected areas on multispecies functional connectivity
papers.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for ecologically well-connected systems, yet progress is tracked with indicators of connectivity state rather than of what protection achieved. We evaluated whether PAs in Colombia maintained multispecies functional connectivity relative to unprotected counterfactuals from 2000 to 2022 and whether the magnitude of their effects reflected the pressure they faced. We grouped 181 bird and mammal species into 12 emergent functional groups (EFGs) based on movement traits and exposure to human modification, modeled their connectivity with omnidirectional circuit theory, and matched protected and unprotected pixels with propensity scores within 6 regional subsystems. For 135 PAs, we estimated effects on standardized connectivity change ([Delta]Z) and on avoided critical loss (connected pixels that became impeded) and classified PAs by avoided loss relative to control loss. Connectivity changed more favorably in PAs than in controls (median & [Delta]Z effect 0.87, 95% CI 0.36-1.60); 72.6% of PAs had positive effects, which were significant in 4 of 6 regions. Protected areas avoided 1.51 percentage points (pp) of critical loss nationally, and avoided loss was positive in all 12 EFGs and significant in 8. However, the presence of an effect overstated its contribution: only 55% of PAs avoided more than 1 pp, and 30% lost more than their controls. Effectiveness increased with pressure, from 39% of PAs under low pressure to 75% under high pressure, where sustainable-use areas accounted for 29 of the 33 effective PAs. Small PAs contained most of the loss expected without protection (median 70%), and regional and national PAs performed alike under similar pressure. Measuring avoided loss relative to pressure shows where protection secures connectivity and where governance must improve, and offers a replicable indicator for the well-connected component of Target 3.

papers.title: Population structure of human-infecting and environmental isolates of Coccidioides immitis, the fungus causing Valley fever
papers.abstract: Coccidioides is a soil-dwelling fungus that can cause serious disease (coccidioidomycosis or Valley fever) when its spores are inhaled. Limiting exposure to environmental spores is critical for disease prevention, yet how Coccidioides is distributed in the soil and where people become exposed remain almost entirely unknown. Here we report the first genomes of environmental isolates of C. immitis, from sampling of rodent burrows in the highly endemic region--California's San Joaquin Valley. We sequenced 16 soil-derived isolates alongside 26 novel patient-derived isolates collected from the same region to investigate genetic structure and diversity in C. immitis, and the potential origins of human infection. We found evidence of regional population structure among environmental C. immitis strains, though with extensive allele sharing between clusters. Most patient isolates derived nearly 100% of their ancestry from a genetic cluster shared with soil isolates, suggesting that the Coccidioides strain inhaled by a human host represents a random draw from the environmental pathogen pool. Further, we found that high levels of genomic diversity in environmental C. immitis are partitioned into effectively clonal lineages within individual rodent burrows, with isolates from neighboring burrows differing by over 13,000 SNPs. Together, these data support a picture of diverse, regionally structured environmental populations of C. immitis, suggesting that strategies to assign patient exposures to general regions within the San Joaquin Valley may be possible.

papers.title: Hypoxia can set the elevational limits of dragonflies
papers.abstract: Oxygen declines by ~10% for each 1000m gained above sea level. Although the impact of low oxygen on endotherms has received considerable attention, we know far less about whether or not hypoxia can set the elevational limits of terrestrial ectotherms. Here, we addressed this question using Nearctic dragonflies. First, we experimentally tested if dragonflies are vulnerable to the low oxygen found at high elevations. Our results show that even resting adults struggle with the PO2 that occurs at the highest elevations where dragonflies are found in Colorado, USA. Second, we used a comparative approach to test if the dragonfly species that can inhabit higher elevations are also more tolerant of low oxygen. Our analysis shows that a species upper elevational limit is precisely predicted by its vulnerability to low oxygen. Collectively, these results provide some of the first evidence that low oxygen can be an important constraint on the elevational maxima of terrestrial ectotherms.

papers.title: Sex in the City: Reproductive Behaviors of Dragonflies across an Urban Landscape
papers.abstract: Anthropogenic cityscapes provide complex habitats that influence animal communication and movement patterns, which are generally understudied in aquatic and semi-aquatic organisms. Community science, referring to public participation in scientific research, is an important tool for recording occurrence records and behavioral observations of understudied urban species. Boise, Idaho (USA), one of the fastest-growing cities in North America, has a long-established community science program for documenting occurrences of the semi-aquatic insect order Odonata (dragonflies and damselflies), making the city an ideal study system for comparing behavioral observations from community science with observations recorded using AI driven iNaturalist. In this study, we test the accuracy of iNaturalist observations and volunteer surveys to characterize dragonfly reproductive behaviors (tandem flight and tandem perching, oviposition, and mating) in the city, and use these observations to determine which dragonflies are using the urban landscape as reproductive habitat. The total numbers of species observations by volunteers and on iNaturalist in Boise were strongly correlated, while reproductive observations showed a strong observational threshold, as reproductive behaviors were rarely identified in less-observed species. iNaturalist tended to underrepresent total occurrences of ''flyer'' species, which rarely perch, while volunteer surveys underrepresented occurrences and reproductive behaviors of a more cyclical species that did not appear to be abundant in the field season in which this study was conducted. Our findings suggest that Boise provides suitable breeding habitat for both migratory and resident dragonflies. Species distribution models of three migratory and three putatively migratory species further demonstrate that these species would be expected in southwestern Idaho regardless of the presence of a city, and have persisted through urban development. This research demonstrates the value of community science in conducting basic research on understudied urban-dwelling species, although findings must be considered alongside potential biases.

papers.title: From individuals to ecosystems: carrion beetle responses to heatwaves impact nutrient cycling
papers.abstract: Climate extremes, such as heatwaves, are becoming more frequent and severe, leading to significant disruptions in key ecosystem processes. The direct effects of heatwaves on these processes have thus received increasing attention, yet the indirect effects of heatwaves, as mediated through animal behavioural responses, are still unknown. Insects play a fundamental role in carrion decomposition by modifying carcasses and regulating nutrient transfer to soils. Understanding how insect responses to climate extremes scale up to ecosystem processes is therefore crucial. In this study, we used a widespread carrion beetle, the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides, to experimentally investigate the direct and indirect effects of a simulated heatwave on carrion decomposition dynamics, and the consequences for soil nutrient cycling. We found that burying beetle presence increased carcass mass loss by 355% under ambient temperatures, and that this was accompanied by significant increases in dissolved organic carbon (+86%), ammonium (+71%), and nitrate (+47%) concentrations. However, the positive effects of burying beetle presence on carcass mass loss were severely diminished by heat stress. Path analyses revealed that this was related to marked reductions in certain beetle behaviours, such as carcass preparation, as well as a reduction in brood size. These behavioural and reproductive shifts were, in turn, linked to decreased soil nitrate concentrations and soil moisture. Together, these findings demonstrate that the indirect effects of heatwaves on decomposition processes, as mediated by shifts in the behaviour and traits of animal ecosystem engineers, can be as important as their direct effects. Such indirect effects must therefore be incorporated into our understanding of how key ecosystem processes respond to climate extremes.

papers.title: Climate change effects on terpene expression differ among populations and have consequences for herbivory in an invasive plant
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT 1. Plant secondary metabolites often moderate interactions with abiotic and biotic factors. For example, secondary metabolites often deter insect herbivores from and influence the extent of damage to plant tissues. However, little is known about how climate change may alter the expression of secondary metabolites and the nature of the resulting effects on plant-herbivore interactions. As climate change continues to shift environmental conditions away from historical norms, climate change effects on plant-herbivore interactions may have important consequences for the range expansion of invasive plants and the efficacy of biocontrol agents across the range. 2. In this study, we examined climate change effects on terpene expression in common tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) in four field transplant sites in Minnesota, U.S.A. that include experimental manipulation of precipitation and temperature. Each transplant site included genotypes from 10 natural populations that span climate variation across Minnesota. We quantified leaf terpene profiles in two years (2024 and 2025) using targeted gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. We surveyed insect herbivory to the same genotypes in experimental field sites to ask how terpene profiles and chemotypes contribute to the likelihood of herbivory. 3. We detected evidence that climate change manipulation altered terpene production and depended on source population. Similarly, the extent of temporal variation in terpene profiles depended upon source population. We also found variation in terpene profiles among sites, further emphasizing the role of the environment in shaping terpene production. These shifts in terpene profiles, in turn, influenced the likelihood of herbivory. Herbivory was higher at the southern compared to northern sites and susceptibility to herbivory was higher in the northern compared to southern populations, particularly at northern sites where average herbivory was lower. The likelihood of herbivory also varied among chemotypes and the frequency of chemotypes varied among source populations, suggesting a complex interplay between the historical and current environments, terpene production, and plant-herbivore interactions. 4. Synthesis. Together, our results suggest a combined role of the abiotic environment and population differentiation in moderating plant-herbivore interactions via shifts and variation in terpene profiles, which may influence invasive range dynamics and complicate the regional management strategies of common tansy.

papers.title: The dynamic face of rarity: tracking species at risk beyond space
papers.abstract: Avoid extinction of rare species is critical for biodiversity conservation. Rabinowitz proposes rare species is pattern that emerge from combination of three parameters: geographical range, habitat specificity and population size. Several papers have been looked to improves this method over last years, but they often neglect the temporal dimension, crucial for understanding the extinction process. This study introduces a dynamic framework that model the three dimensions of rarity as a continuous three-dimensional space, integrating vector-based representations and an ecological vector field to quantify rarity, temporal dynamics, displacement and equilibrium. Derivative equations are used to describe the temporal evolution in that system which is integrate to account the shift in that space. This framework allows to reinterpret ecological change as a trajectory though space, where each axis corresponds to an ecological dimension. This multidimensional representation distinguishes intrinsic rarity from extinction risk and can identify demographic declines, habitat restriction, or range contraction. The method can be applied to a single species or a set of species, using short or long sampling time intervals. A test across freshwater fish, birds, amphibians, and terrestrial plants showed that rarity dimensions can change independently among species. By monitoring the shifts in this dimension simultaneity, we can plan the conservation by priority species that are shaking their dimensions over time. Unlike static assessments that already exist, this method provides a nuanced understanding of a rare species vulnerability as a dynamic representation of temporal changes. An R package and application guide are provided, helping conservation practitioners use this approach.

papers.title: How does the community structure of dung beetles affect ecosystem functions? Modeling of secondary seed dispersal and seedling establishment.
papers.abstract: Dung beetles are associated with diverse ecosystem functions. However, their populations are declining globally, raising concerns about the loss of ecosystem functions. Among these services, secondary seed dispersal is crucial for plant recruitment and movement. To reveal the relationship between community composition and ecosystem function, I developed a novel mathematical model simulating seedling establishment that accounts for seed dispersal by two functional groups (tunnelers and rollers), seed predation, and among-seedling competition. The model revealed that when seed predators were absent, rollers contributed more to seedling establishment than tunnelers; consequently, communities with a high proportion of rollers and a low proportion of tunnelers maximized the number of established seedlings. Under high predation pressure, tunneler-abundant communities yielded greater seedling establishment. Under intermediate predation pressure, the relative contributions of the two functional groups depended on the intensity of among-seedling competition: tunnelers enhanced establishment when competition was weak, whereas rollers excelled when competition was strong. This study provides the first mathematical framework for dung beetle-mediated secondary seed dispersal, advancing our understanding of the links between community composition and ecosystem functioning. These findings offer critical insights for anthropogenic biodiversity management, such as the conservation and introduction of dung beetle communities.

papers.title: Hidden grassland productivity from overlooked herbivore impacts
papers.abstract: Grasslands cover approximately 40% of Earth's land surface and contribute substantially to terrestrial primary production. Despite widespread grazing, field estimates of grassland aboveground net primary productivity commonly overlook two grazing-related processes: biomass consumed by herbivores and post-grazing compensatory growth. The magnitude and direction of the resulting biases remain unclear. Here we quantified these biases using a 3-year yak grazing experiment on the Tibetan Plateau, a meta-analysis of 152 grazing experiments across China, and a global synthesis of 212 paired observations from 58 studies. Overlooking biomass consumed by herbivores consistently underestimated productivity by 34-51%. By contrast, overlooking grazing-induced compensation generated smaller but more variable biases, ranging from 29% underestimation to 19% overestimation, mainly reflecting contrasting compensatory responses under rotational versus continuous grazing. These findings show that overlooking grazing-mediated processes introduces substantial, process-dependent biases in grassland productivity estimates, underscoring the need to incorporate these processes into ecosystem and climate assessments.

papers.title: Mercury bioaccumulation varies across breeding-site height and life-history traits in Amazonian phytotelm-breeding frogs
papers.abstract: Mercury (Hg) concentrations in the environment have significantly increased in the Amazon. Despite the observed deleterious effects on freshwater wildlife, the impacts of Hg contamination in phytotelmata (i.e., waterbodies contained in plant structures) and the species therein remain undocumented. We investigated the effects of Hg contamination on a phytotelm-breeding frog community in an otherwise pristine rainforest in French Guiana. Total Hg concentrations were measured in 28 pools at different heights (i.e. ground to canopy), and in the bodies of 103 tadpoles from five species with contrasting life histories. Tadpoles from ground pools had higher Hg concentrations than those from arboreal pools, revealing a vertical gradient in Hg contamination; tadpoles from species with slow development and parental care (i.e., tadpole transport) exhibited higher Hg concentrations than those of species with fast development without parental care. Finally, although Hg burdens were not associated with oxidative DNA levels, individuals reaching metamorphosis exhibited lower DNA damage than early-stage tadpoles, possibly reflecting reduced oxidative damage resulting from cellular remodelling undergone during metamorphosis, or selective mortality processes. Our findings highlight the joint influence of habitat type and life-history traits on Hg accumulation and that, even in pristine forests, Hg exposure varies strongly across microhabitats and species.

papers.title: Avian uropygial secretions as a novel bioinsecticide for mosquito vector control
papers.abstract: Background: Malaria control relies heavily on interventions targeting mosquito vectors, but the rapid emergence of insecticide resistance threatens the effectiveness of existing approaches. Identifying novel, effective, and environmentally sustainable insecticides is therefore a priority. Birds produce uropygial secretions with well-documented antimicrobial properties, but their potential insecticidal activity against mosquitoes, including malaria vectors, remains unexplored. Methods: We evaluated the insecticidal activity of uropygial secretions from wild house sparrows (Passer domesticus) against the malaria vector Anopheles stephensi and four additional mosquito species of medical importance (Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus, Culex pipiens, and Culiseta longiareolata). A total of 2,293 adult mosquitoes were tested using CDC bottle bioassays at three secretion concentrations (0.5, 0.25, and 0.125) and an untreated control. Mosquito mortality was monitored for 120 min. Results: Uropygial secretions caused substantial mosquito knockdown/mortality, with effects increasing with concentration and exposure time. Susceptibility differed significantly among species after 120 min. Notably, An. stephensi was particularly susceptible, reaching knockdown/mortality of 92%, 94%, and 83% at 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125 concentrations, respectively. Conclusions: Our findings provide the first experimental evidence that avian uropygial secretions possess direct insecticidal activity against mosquitoes and identify them as a previously overlooked source of naturally derived insecticidal compounds. The high susceptibility of An. stephensi highlights their potential relevance for developing novel bioinsecticides for malaria vector control.

papers.title: Global failure to track international biodiversity targets on islands
papers.abstract: Islands harbour exceptional biodiversity but face severe threats, making their conservation crucial to achieving the goals and targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. We therefore evaluated whether existing indicators can track progress toward the Framework's 23 targets across islands worldwide. We screened 504 biodiversity and socioeconomic indicators from the official framework and other global initiatives, retaining 47 indicators. Historical time series from 1950 onward were modelled and projected to 2030. Indicators were also classified using the Driver-Pressure-State-Impact-Response (DPSIR) and Theory of Change (ToC). Results showed uneven progress: eight targets improved across all available indicators, while ten displayed conflicting trends. Nearly half of the indicators focused on policy and management responses showed improvement, whereas trends in biodiversity pressures and states were mixed. Critically, 15 of 23 targets (65%) lacked a suitable headline indicator, and five targets had no indicator at all. Notably, Targets 2 and 8, addressing ecosystem restoration and climate change impacts, respectively, lacked island indicators entirely. Over half of the available indicators (29 of 47; 62%) were reported at the national level, limiting their applicability to subnational island jurisdictions and potentially obscuring differences between mainland and island conditions. Most targets also lacked quantitative objectives, limiting evaluation of whether the rate of change is sufficient to meet the targets by 2030. We recommend island-level reporting, island-specific indicators, and quantitative benchmarks tailored to island needs.

papers.title: Intra- and interspecific relationships of alpine ungulates reorganise along a wolf recolonisation gradient
papers.abstract: Apex predators are recovering across many ecosystems after decades of decline, yet whether their return can restore ecological interactions disrupted by their loss remains poorly understood. Here, we used the ongoing recolonisation of grey wolves (Canis lupus) in the south-eastern Alps as a natural gradient of predator recovery to examine how predation risk and human disturbance shape relationships among red deer (Cervus elaphus), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), and Alpine chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra). Across a gradient of time since wolf establishment, roe deer increasingly occupied sites without red deer, suggesting predator recovery alters relationships between prey species. Red deer also formed larger groups, consistent with a shift in collective behaviour under increased predation risk. Human disturbance also affected group formation in red deer and chamois. Together, these findings show that prey community structure can vary with wolf recovery, even in human-dominated landscapes, through altered associations among species and grouping within species.

papers.title: The conservation effectiveness of Indigenous and local community governance
papers.abstract: Effective governance of natural areas is central to conserving biodiversity and Earth's life support systems, including climate regulation and food and water provisioning. Understanding the relative effectiveness of different governance options is thus critical. We conducted a global meta-analysis of 409 cases in 42 countries, comparing ecological outcomes over time in areas governed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities versus conventional governance approaches. Outcomes in community-governed areas matched those in conventional fully protected areas and exceeded those in partially protected and unprotected areas. Communities with legal land title had better outcomes than communities without title. We provide the strongest evidence to date that ecological outcomes of Indigenous and community governance meet or exceed those of other area-based conservation approaches and that titling strengthens these outcomes.

papers.title: Beyond the urban surface: bird-borne sensing reveals the atmospheric structure of urban heat
papers.abstract: Urban heat is commonly characterized near ground level, while its vertical atmospheric structure remains difficult to observe across cities. We used bird-borne temperature sensors on homing pigeons (Columba livia) and yellow-legged gulls (Larus michahellis) to investigate the horizontal, vertical and daytime structure of the lower urban atmosphere over Rome. The dataset comprised 61,917 air-temperature observations from 47 individuals of gulls and pigeons, spanning 17 km and altitudes up to 400 m above ground level. Generalized additive models related air temperature to distance from the city centre, altitude, time of day, land cover, tree-patch area and topography, and reconstructed three-dimensional temperature fields. Air temperature showed a centre-to-periphery gradient that weakened with altitude and through the daytime period. At 20 m above ground level, its magnitude declined from -0.40 {degrees}C km--1 at 09:00 to -0.30 {degrees}C km--1 at 13:00 and -0.19 {degrees}C km--1 at 17:00, with weaker gradients at higher altitudes. Reconstructed isothermal boundaries showed a complementary vertical pattern. At 13:00, median heights decreased from 135 m for the 34 {degrees}C boundary to 76 m for 35 {degrees}C and 37 m for 36 {degrees}C. The 34 {degrees}C boundary reached its greatest extent around midday, rising from 57 m at 09:00 to 135 m at 13:00 before declining to 14 m at 17:00. Horizontal thermal contrast and the vertical development of high-temperature air represent complementary dimensions of urban heat. Bird-borne sensing offers a promising approach for resolving three-dimensional atmospheric temperature patterns that conventional monitoring networks cannot capture.

papers.title: DroneMegaDetector, A Generalised Model For Detecting Large Mammals In Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Large-scale drone surveys can generate imagery across substantial geographic areas, but automated analysis remains challenging because animal appearance, target density, imaging conditions and target scale can vary considerably between surveys. We present a general-purpose RF-DETR Medium object detector developed for large-scale aerial drone imagery and evaluate its ability to generalise across taxa, environments and survey conditions. Unlike specialist counting systems that primarily return point detections, the proposed detector produces explicit bounding boxes, providing a spatial representation that can support counting as well as downstream detection, classification and tracking workflows. We evaluated the detector on an internal held-out test set and independent external datasets spanning cattle, birds, caribou and hippopotamuses, together with imagery acquired under substantially different survey conditions. On the comparative Cattle dataset, RF-DETR matched OWL across the reported point-localisation and counting metrics, while on Caribou it achieved almost identical point-based detection performance and similar aggregate counting error. Performance varied across the broader external benchmark, with reduced transfer to unseen avian imagery and differences between models across datasets. At high altitude on SAVMAP, all evaluated approaches experienced substantial performance degradation, demonstrating a shared limitation associated with small target scale. Overall, the results show that a general-purpose detector trained on heterogeneous drone imagery can provide competitive localisation and counting performance across diverse datasets while retaining explicit bounding-box outputs. The trained model weights and inference code are provided online to support reproducible large-scale aerial wildlife monitoring and further development of drone-based computer-vision workflows.

papers.title: Species ecology, behavior, and substrate type shape eDNA detection of mammals at savanna waterholes
papers.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly used to monitor terrestrial mammal biodiversity, yet factors that influence detection probability in such systems remain poorly understood. Substrates in and around freshwater drinking areas represent particularly promising eDNA sampling points to capture terrestrial biodiversity, especially in arid and semi-arid landscapes. However, eDNA detection probabilities are expected to depend strongly on the frequency and intensity of animal interaction with the sampled substrate at these watering holes. We combined camera trapping with eDNA metabarcoding to investigate drivers of mammal eDNA detection at savanna waterholes in South Africa (Botsalano Game Reserve) over several weeks during both wet and dry seasons and evaluated the effects of species behavior (interaction intensity with water), species traits, environmental covariates and substrate type (water versus sediment) on eDNA detection probabilities. Camera trapping detected 30 mammal species, whereas eDNA metabarcoding detected 40 species, with 25 species being shared between methods. Body size increased detection probability using camera traps but not using eDNA metabarcoding. eDNA detection was strongly influenced by trophic level, with herbivores exhibiting significantly higher eDNA detection rates than omnivores and carnivores. eDNA detection probability further increased with behavioral water interaction intensity, social group size, visitation frequency, the number of observed individuals, and declined with time elapsed since the last visit of the respective species. A fine-scale spatial analysis within the water bodies revealed that eDNA deposition is highly localized. Substrate type had a pronounced effect, with sediment samples reflecting more long-term mammal activity, whereas water samples reflected more recent interactions and were more sensitive to environmental conditions. Samples collected at wildlife trails exhibited similar patterns, with trophic level and spatial proximity to the trail both increasing detection rates.

papers.title: Interactive effects of land use change and climate drive the decline of a threatened boreal forest orchid in Finland
papers.abstract: Land use and climate change are two of the greatest threats to biodiversity globally. However, their interactive effects remain poorly understood. In the boreal forest biome, where species are experiencing increasing pressures from forest management and climate change, improved understanding of these effects is urgently needed. Here, we assess the impacts of forest loss and both baseline and changing late spring climatic conditions on the extinction probability of a threatened boreal forest orchid, Calypso bulbosa. We use a unique dataset consisting of 1,006 C. bulbosa occurrence sites located in Finland, historical aerial images, and climatic data spanning the last 60 years. Our results reveal that forest loss, at the local rather than landscape-scale, and both the site-specific baseline climatic conditions and their change over time influence the extinction probability of C. bulbosa. These effects were mainly interactive with greater temporal increase in rainfall ameliorating and greater baseline rainfall exacerbating the negative effect of forest loss on the species persistence. Furthermore, greater baseline snow depth ameliorated this negative effect. We also found some statistical support for independent effects of baseline thermal sum and its change over time, but their ecological relevance was interpreted as minor. Overall, our results align with the expectation that forest loss can modify the exposure of forest-dependent species to climatic conditions, thus altering their vulnerability to climate change.

papers.title: Supplemental water modulates pollinator visitation on resource-rich plant species
papers.abstract: Urban green spaces provide important floral resources for pollinators, and supplemental watering can improve the abundance and quality of these resources. However, increasing frequency and intensity of drought under climate change create tradeoffs between ecological benefits and water conservation. Manipulating the timing and duration of irrigation may offer a way of enhancing floral traits that support pollinator communities while moderating water use. Focusing on two resource-rich native plant species, Phacelia californica and Helenium puberulum, we examined how the addition of supplemental water in spring and summer affects floral traits and pollinator visitation. We examined mechanisms that may govern the effects of supplemental watering on pollinator visitation, namely the number of flowers, nectar volume, nectar sucrose concentration, and corolla length. Overall, plant individuals receiving more water were visited by more pollinators. In both plant species, this was apparently mediated by floral abundance; individual plants with more flowers received more visitors, though effects of watering varied slightly between the two plant species and the insect visitor taxa. Water additions in spring increased pollinator visitation per plant on P. californica, but visitation rates per flower did not differ among treatments. Responses among pollinator groups varied, with effects driven primarily by sweat bees (family: Halictidae) and bumble bees (Bombus species), while honeybee visitation was consistent across treatments. Our results suggest that insects prefer to visit supplementally watered P. californica plants. Because honeybee visitation did not vary by treatment, supplemental water may disproportionately benefit native pollinators, including bumblebees, which are imperiled. Similar to P. californica, Helenium puberulum plants watered in spring and summer had the most flowers and the most floral visitors per plant and per flower. Spring-watering H. puberulum did not have a significant effect on flower production but did increase insect visitation per flower. Overall, our results emphasize that irrigation and other avenues of water addition are key drivers of flower production and insect visitation, such that homeowners who wish to conserve water must weigh effects on pollinators with the need to conserve water in arid climates.

papers.title: Integrating morphological and molecular approaches to assess photosynthetic species diversity in the Venice Lagoon
papers.abstract: The Venice Lagoon is the largest transitional environment in the Mediterranean Sea and an important biodiversity hotspot. However, it is under increasing climate and anthropogenic pressures, highlighting the need for long-term monitoring of its biodiversity. Three monitoring campaigns were conducted between 2023 and 2025, sampling seaweeds, seagrasses and halophytes. Samples were identified using an integrated morphological and molecular approach, with morphological traits guiding the selection of the most appropriate DNA-barcoding markers. High-quality sequences were obtained for 50% of the samples and compared with reference databases. To improve identification reliability, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed for each major taxonomic group to assess clustering patterns and sequence relationships. Two independent species-delimitation methods, ASAP and GMYC, were also applied. Overall, 81 taxa were identified, 13 belonging to Chlorophyta, 11 to Heterokontophyta, 28 to Rhodophyta, and 29 to Tracheophyta. We further conducted a targeted survey on Sporobolus species using the trnL-trnF marker and genome-size estimates to distinguish between native and non-indigenous ones. The presence of S. x townsendii was confirmed in the central and southern lagoon, while the non-indigenous S. anglicus was more prevalent than the native S. maritimus.

papers.title: Large-scale exposure of southern seabirds to avian cholera Pasteurella multocida: scavengers as sentinels at different spatial scales
papers.abstract: Seabird communities represent spatially structured social networks within which potential sentinels could inform us where multi-host pathogens could be present. Pasteurella multocida, the agent of avian cholera, is responsible for recurrent massive seabird mortality events on remote Amsterdam Island, Southern Indian Ocean, but little is known about its broad spatial occurrence. To explore its distribution and whether avian scavengers and predators could be used as sentinels, we screened 18 southern seabird species from 11 islands for antibodies against P. multocida (2634 plasma samples). We detected widespread but heterogeneous exposure among host populations. High seroprevalences were found in widely roaming predators and scavengers (giant petrels (Macronectes spp), and brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus)), which could represent efficient sentinels at broad scales. Antibodies were also detected over a series of years in a non-migratory scavenger, the lesser sheathbill (Chionis minor) and an abundant penguin species, the king penguin (Aptenodytes patagonicus), suggesting that the bacterium was circulating locally at some sites. This broad scale serological screening of whole seabird host communities provides critical information to assess disease emergence risks in the context of global change.

papers.title: Decomposition trajectories in mixed-species leaf litter in cool-temperate deciduous forest with understory dwarf bamboo
papers.abstract: Litter decomposition plays a central role in nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems, but the effects of species mixing on decomposition of individual litter species remain poorly understood. We conducted a two-year litterbag experiment in a cool-temperate deciduous forest in northern Japan using litter from two dominant canopy tree species (oak and birch) and the dominant understory bamboo (Sasa). Single-species and mixed-species litterbags were used to examine litter mass loss, litter chemistry (carbon, nitrogen, and lignin), and microbial communities assessed by phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) analysis. Oak and birch litter decomposed significantly faster than Sasa litter, whereas decomposition rate constants did not differ between the two deciduous tree species. Changes in litter chemistry relative to mass loss were similar between oak and birch but differed markedly in Sasa, indicating a distinct decomposition trajectory of Sasa. Total microbial biomass increased rapidly during the early stage of decomposition in all litter types owing to fungal colonization, whereas the fungal-to-bacterial PLFA ratio was substantially lower in Sasa litter than in deciduous tree litter. Species mixing had no significant overall non-additive effect on decomposition, although mixtures of oak and birch tended to accelerate decomposition, whereas mixtures including Sasa tended to suppress it. These changes in decomposition rate were accompanied by corresponding changes in microbial biomass, while decomposition trajectories remained largely unchanged within each litter species. Our results suggest that Sasa contributes a distinct decomposition process in cool-temperate forests and that species mixing primarily modifies decomposition rates rather than the sequence of chemical transformations during decomposition.

papers.title: Soil nitrogen dynamics in riparian zones of two Arctic rivers
papers.abstract: Riparian zones act as protective buffers, filtering land-to-river nutrient inputs through retention and nitrogen (N) gas losses. While rapid Arctic warming and permafrost thaw may enhance terrestrial nutrient inputs to aquatic systems, comprehensive assessments of N cycling in Arctic riparian soils are lacking. Conventionally, these zones are considered inactive due to N limitation of Arctic soils and low temperatures, leaving their N cycling unexplored. To address this, we investigated N pools and turnover processes in riparian zones of two Arctic rivers in Finland and Greenland. We combined measurements of the extractable N pool and in-situ nitrous oxide (N2O) flux with 15N-labeling techniques to quantify gross mineralization, nitrification, potential denitrification, and potential dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA). Our findings reveal that mineral N cycling in high-latitude riparian zones is more active than previously assumed. Despite low temperatures and low to intermediate soil organic carbon content, we found high gross N mineralization rates, alongside detectable rates of gross nitrification and potential DNRA. We attribute the unexpectedly high N activity in C-poor soils to low C/N ratios, which create a stoichiometric imbalance, thereby enhancing N mineralization. The presence or absence of vegetation largely determined the dominance and magnitude of these pathways. While dense vascular plant cover was associated with higher extractable N pools and gross mineralization rate, low nitrification rates and elevated DNRA potential indicated a tight N cycle. Conversely, sparsely vegetated patches with cryptogamic biocrusts acted as N2O hotspots. In bare sandy soils adjacent to the river, we found high gross nitrification rate and detectable N2O losses, possibly driven by riverine organic N inputs. Taken together, this research shows that Arctic riparian zones may play an important role in reducing terrestrial N inputs to the rivers, which should be considered when studying the fate of N in the rapidly changing Arctic.

papers.title: From tropical rainforests to scorching deserts: biogeography shapes climate-change plasticity in Australian rainbowfishes
papers.abstract: Thermal tolerance and the plasticity of regulatory mechanisms are likely to influence biodiversity persistence under global warming. Continental-scale assessments of physiological resilience and gene expression plasticity within a closely related clade are rare, yet they could reveal how bioregional climatic history shapes vulnerability to climate warming. We used a comparative approach across five climatic ecotypes of Australian rainbowfishes (tropical rainforest, tropical savannah, subtropical, desert, and temperate) to investigate variation in thermal tolerance and gene expression plasticity in response to warming. We reconstructed phylogenetic relationships among these ecotypes, estimated their ecological niches and environmental warming tolerance, and experimentally measured CTMAX and global gene expression responses to a projected summer heat event. Closely related ecotypes showed divergent bioclimatic niches, contrasting sensitivities to warming, and extensive but idiosyncratic expression responses to heat stress. Plastic responses to warming, including in key heat stress genes, were positively associated with thermal tolerance across ecotypes. The tropical savannah and subtropical ecotypes, both from environmentally variable bioregions, showed extensive transcriptional responses to warming and high thermal tolerance. The desert ecotype was intermediate for both traits, whereas the temperate ecotype showed the most limited transcriptional response and lowest thermal tolerance. In contrast, the tropical rainforest ecotype showed limited plasticity, potentially reflecting local adaptation to milder, more stable conditions and more specialised thermal responses. Our findings support the hypothesis that bioregional climatic history shapes broad patterns of climate resilience, including thermal tolerance and transcriptional plasticity, and may influence which combinations of traits are favoured under future climates.

papers.title: Two decades of Novel Ecosystems: Literature analysis of topics, trends and connectivity
papers.abstract: 1. As human-driven climate change and other anthropogenic forces produce widespread impacts on biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, many ecosystems are shifting into unprecedented, novel states. The Novel Ecosystem Concept (NEC), formalized in 2006, was developed as an alternative framework for managing "novel ecosystems", human-altered systems that are challenging to restore to their historical state. In the years since, the NEC has been proposed as a broader lens for ecosystem management under ongoing global change. 2. We evaluated how the uptake and potential of the NEC have been realized over time using a bibliometric and linguistic toolkit. Using bibliometric data from the Web of Science, we clustered 40,914 applied ecology papers published between 2006 and 2025 into twenty research topics based on language use. We quantified the volume of NEC research within each topic, rates of publication over time, and cross-topic connectivity proxied by citations. 3. We found NEC research in most of the topics of applied ecology, particularly invasion biology, ecosystem services, soil research and studies of freshwater, urban and marine systems. In contrast, several major conservation-focused topics, including protected areas, threatened species, and human-wildlife interactions, contained little research with an explicit link to novel ecosystems. Publication rates increased across all topics, although growth slowed over time. At the same time, NEC research became more focused into ecosystem-specific topics, especially marine ecosystems. NEC research across different topics was well-connected by citations, with papers more likely to cite each other when they used similar language. 4. Overall, the NEC does not appear to have expanded beyond its origins in restoration to become a broadly applied framework across conservation and ecosystem management. Instead, the concepts behind the NEC have been integrated into restoration and management frameworks grappling with climate and other anthropogenic change, while "novelty" is emerging as a powerful quantitative variable for measuring ecological change over space and time. Our results highlight the potential value of bibliometric and linguistic tools to deconstruct the ecological literature to inform what we can, or should, do to intervene for benefit of nature and people.

papers.title: Community assembly dynamics in a regulated stream: Insights from environmental DNA
papers.abstract: Degradation of freshwater habitats, including the alteration of natural flow regimes by impoundment, is a major threat to native fishes. When dam removal is not possible, management actions to recover natural flow regimes can benefit native species, but monitoring community responses is crucial to show efficacy. We used eDNA metabarcoding to quantify spatiotemporal trends in fish assemblages along the longitudinal profile of a regulated stream where a court-ratified environmental flows framework is used to benefit native fishes. At a subset of sites, we also compared eDNA results with concurrent surveys conducted using long-term standardized fisheries monitoring techniques to evaluate concordance. From 59 eDNA samples collected over approximately 2 years, we detected 26 fish taxa, including 8 native species, with 25 taxa resolving to species level using a custom reference sequence database; one taxon could not be resolved between closely related species. Fish assemblages varied predictably along the longitudinal profile of the stream and by season (fall and spring). Diversity indices were higher at downstream sites and in fall, reflecting greater richness of warm-water non-native species. Evenness was similar among sites but shifts in species ranks suggests reordering processes drive spatiotemporal variation in assembly. Gradient forest analysis identified thirteen species associated with spatiotemporal gradients, including both native cold-water species and non-native warm-water species. Overall, eDNA results were concordant with conventional fisheries monitoring but eDNA detected significantly greater species richness through increased detection of rare species. eDNA results align with long-term monitoring that demonstrated assemblage shifts in upper, but not lower stream reaches, and extends the insights into spatial responses, species reordering, and ecology of rare species. These findings demonstrate the value of eDNA as a complementary tool for understanding community assembly dynamics, including responses to stream rehabilitation and ecosystem management.

papers.title: Human-wildlife conflict shows shared spatial predictors across ecological and geographic contexts
papers.abstract: Human-wildlife conflict (HWC) is a global challenge for biodiversity conservation, food security, and human well-being. Effective management towards human-wildlife coexistence, recognized as a priority in Target 4 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, requires understanding the drivers of HWC. However, the strong influence of local human and ecological context means that most HWC research focuses on individual case studies, limiting transferability of patterns across contexts. Here, we link local contexts and transferable drivers by testing whether HWC exhibits an intermediate level of organization, in which local predictor profiles are structured by broader ecological, geographic, and taxonomic contexts. After compiling ~11,000 conflict incidents, we construct and compare random forest models across 29 mammalian HWC scenarios spanning diverse species, conflict types, biomes, and continents to identify contexts in which predictor profiles converge. While predictors varied among individual conflicts, HWC scenarios were organized by shared context: conflicts occurring within the same biome tended to have similar predictor profiles, with continent and taxonomic group providing additional structure. Proximity to protected areas was the most consistently important predictor of HWC globally. The likelihood of conflict increased with human population density across nearly all scales and contexts, while distance to roads was also an important predictor in many contexts. Together, these results demonstrate an intermediate level of organization in HWC that reconciles case-specific variation with broader patterns across biomes, continents, and taxonomic groups. This framework provides a basis for scaling mitigation strategies beyond individual case studies while avoiding one-size-fits-all approaches.

papers.title: Long-term Population Dynamics and Conservation of Proboscis Monkeys (Nasalis larvatus) in the Lower Kinabatangan, Sabah, Malaysia
papers.abstract: Long-term ecological monitoring is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of conservation actions for long-lived tropical primates, yet few studies have integrated repeated population censuses with habitat-change analyses. We evaluated long-term population and habitat dynamics of the endangered proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) in the Lower Kinabatangan, Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, by integrating a landscape-wide population survey conducted in 2025 with previous surveys from 2005 and 2014, long-term monitoring at three representative sites, and spatial analyses of land-use and land-cover change. Standardized late-afternoon boat-based surveys covering approximately 223 km of the Kinabatangan River and its tributaries recorded an estimated 2,420 individuals in 174 social groups, representing an increase of approximately 66% and 72% respectively compared with the 2005 survey. Group sizes (number of individuals per social group) remained largely unchanged despite the overall increase in population size. Long-term monitoring at three representative sites indicated stable population trajectories throughout the study period. Habitat analyses further revealed an increase in natural vegetation and limited conversion of forest to oil palm within protected areas between 2005 and 2025. Together, these independent lines of evidence indicate that the Lower Kinabatangan proboscis monkey population has recovered while maintaining overall demographic stability under long-term habitat protection. Nevertheless, substantial areas of suitable habitat remain outside the protected-area network, highlighting opportunities for additional habitat restoration and improved landscape connectivity. Our findings demonstrate the value of integrating long-term ecological monitoring with landscape-scale habitat assessment to inform adaptive conservation management in fragmented tropical landscapes.

papers.title: Territorial risk of high pathogenicity avian influenza in France is associated with farmed species diversity
papers.abstract: Animal infectious diseases threaten food security, livestock production and public health. While disease prevention strategies typically target risk factors associated with high-competence hosts or environmental conditions, we hypothesise that lower-competence species can reduce disease risk by diluting effective contact rates between farms. Using spatial statistical models calibrated on three successive French high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics (2020-2023), we show that greater local diversity of livestock farms, including cattle and pig farms, is associated with significantly lower HPAI risk. Moreover, we show that the positive association between duck houses and HPAI risk weakens as the number of less-competent non-duck poultry houses increases, revealing a dilution effect within poultry production systems. These findings suggest that livestock diversity is a previously overlooked determinant of disease spread and open new research avenues on territorial diversification to complement traditional approaches for the long-term control of high-impact animal infectious diseases.

papers.title: Warming responses of microbial respiration emerge from spatially structured species interactions
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are the main drivers of global carbon cycling. Yet, predicting their respiratory responses to warming is challenging because the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we developed a spatially explicit model, integrating single-cell metabolism with metabolic exchange and endogenous heat production, to disentangle the mechanisms driving community-level temperature responses. We reveal that mutualism amplifies respiratory temperature sensitivity compared to isolated taxa, as exchanged metabolites sustain a secondary growth phase with higher respiratory demand, and this phase creates disproportionately large CO2; emissions under warming (apparent activation energy Ea; increases from 0.65 to 0.77 eV). Spatial structure amplifies this further through threshold effects, whereby diffusion limitation shifts from constraining to enabling mutualistic benefits as metabolic rates increase with temperature (Ea; increases to 1.18 {+/-} 0.09 eV). Endogenous heat production drives additional amplification through positive feedback between local temperature rises and resource turnover rates (Ea; further increasing to 1.78 {+/-} 0.14 eV). Collectively, our results demonstrate that community-level temperature responses are not determined by enzyme kinetics alone but emerge from the interplay of ecological, physical, and metabolic interactions. Our model provides a general framework for understanding the combined effects of the underlying mechanisms on microbial temperature responses. Future climate carbon models should incorporate these considerations to improve predictions.
